projectOutComesReport:
Room temperature electrochemical conversion of CO2 gas has been attracting large number of interests from numerous researchers as a highly potent technology sustainable and decentralized chemical manufacturing. Current state of electrochemical CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) technology consists of CO2 capturing and purification process form its source, CO2 conversion process to high value product, and product purification process from remaining electrolyte or byproducts. This project aims to construct an integrated platform that allows direct conversion of CO2 from delocalized sources into high-purity liquid fuels. It specifically targets to enhance the efficiency and versatility of CO2 capture and release process, design stable and efficient CO2RR device, and remove the energy-intensive product purification step.

 

This project focuses on three major objectives: (1) Enhance solid electrolyte CO2RR technology by designing selective CO2RR catalysts and conductive electrolyte. (2) Explore electrochemical CO2 capture technology which utilizes new redox active chemical species. (3) Understand and construct an electrochemical modular system coupling CO2RR and CO2 capture devices for a continuous workflow of waste gas in and pure liquid fuel solutions out.

 

The enhancement of solid electrolyte CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) technology was explored at multiple levels in this project. From the perspective of device design and fabrication, the project addressed the issue of carbon utilization in CO2 electrolyzers by implementing carbon recovery technology that leverages carbonate chemistry and its interactions with the membrane surface during electrolysis. Additionally, the project revisited carbonate chemistry to identify it as a factor influencing the distribution of products between CO2RR and carbon monoxide reduction reaction (CORR). Furthermore, the project demonstrated a solid electrolyte reactor-driven CO2 capture technology that utilizes the aforementioned carbonate chemistry.

 

This project undertook initiatives to synthesize solid electrolytes aimed at enhancing the performance of solid electrolyte CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) technology. The project demonstrated three different types of solid electrolyte designs for CO2RR: sulfonated silica, immobilized and self-contained ion-exchange particle sheets, and covalent organic framework (COF)-based solid electrolytes. Each type of solid electrolyte was synthesized to meet the high conductivity, stability, and selectivity requirements essential for electrolyzers, with each exhibiting distinct advantages in their respective applications.

 

This project focused on discovering new and effective redox pairs for electrochemical CO2 capture. It introduced a novel poly(quinone) that serves as an efficient redox pair for capturing and releasing CO2 molecules from various sources. The investigation involved both experimental and theoretical approaches, illustrating how tools such as density functional theory can be used to screen different redox reactions and assess their interactions with CO2 molecules. The project also developed new synthesis methods for these poly(quinone) moieties, which were successfully incorporated into heterogeneous electrodes for the electrochemical capture and release of CO2. This work broadens the scope of redox-active carbon dioxide sorbents.

 

Ultimately, these projects have a broad impact by integrating and advancing lab-scale CO2 capture and utilization technologies into a cohesive system that converts waste gas directly into valuable commodities. Additionally, the project included community outreach through an initiative called “Energy Exploration Academy,” which engaged middle and high school students to familiarize them with energy and electrochemistry. Finally, the NSF project provided training for graduate students and postdoctoral scholars in the fields of carbon capture and utilization.

abstractText:
Authentication is one of the fundamental primitives to establish security in ubiquitous systems. The current best practice for authentication relies upon cryptography and secure keys. Such an approach can hardly be scaled to emerging applications due to its high-power consumption and vulnerabilities to physical and cryptographic attacks. Strong Physically Unclonable Function (SPUF) promises a lightweight and secure authentication method based on physical disorders. So far, SPUFs with the desired security properties has only been demonstrated with optics or biology. But it is not practical to integrate them with electronics in mobile and ubiquitous systems. This project explores technologies to enable secure and practical SPUFs on silicon chips, which addresses the needs for security solutions in emerging ubiquitous electronics. The project also includes training and teaching graduate and undergraduate students on hardware security.

This project aims to emulate the proven optically disordered SPUF system with an electrical percolation system built on CMOS platforms for authentication. The inter-disciplinary project will be carried out with three objectives: CMOS-compatible electrical percolation nanostructures; CMOS readout circuits and alternative integration strategies; system design and assessment of proof-of-principle SPUFs. The project includes analysis and optimization of the cross-layer design space involving the degree of uncorrelation for nanostructures, the measurement resolution of circuits, and the complexity of encoding schemes. Overall, the project can potentially create a radically different and complete solution to the challenge of authenticating ubiquitous hardware devices.

projectOutComesReport:
Cybersecurity is a primary challenge in the era of ubiquitous electronic sensors and computers, with cryptographic algorithms and secret keys being the current go-to safeguards. However, with technological advancements, these measures are becoming increasingly vulnerable and resource-consuming for ubiquitous devices. Strong Physically Unclonable Function (SPUF) has emerged as a revolutionary foundation for cybersecurity that is immune from cryptoanalysis, advances in mathematics and computers (even quantum computers), or physical probing and side-channel attacks. It also achieves information theoretical security as defined by C. Shannon. Last but not least, due to its physical nature and tight bonding to a specific chip, SPUF enables novel and essential security applications like chip supply chain integrity that cannot be achieved with conventional cryptographic systems. 

Despite its great potential, the original SPUF demonstration with an optical scattering system is bulky, expensive, and power-consuming, making it unsuitable for mobile, edge, and ubiquitous devices. For more than a decade, researchers have been exploring a plethora of CMOS and post-CMOS electronic devices and circuits, as well as optical features in silk fibers, ink-jet prints, gold films, diamond particles, and biological systems to build a compact and secure SPUF. However, none of these efforts have been successful due to the fundamentally limited density of entropy sources harnessed in these systems. 

The goal of this project was to study the feasibility of building a monolithically integrated SPUF capable of producing more than a billion uncorrelated and reliable CRPs with low energy consumption and tamper resistance. Through extensive theoretical analysis and experimental optimizations, this project demonstrated the feasibility of utilizing high-density physical entropy sources to realize billions independent and identically distributed challenge-response pairs (CRPs) within a few millimeter square of chip area. Measurement of fabricated SPUF samples demonstrate CRPs with excellent randomness, independence, stability across a wide temperature range, and scalability towards sufficient CRPs for lifetime authentications within a tiny chip. The statistical properties of the CRPs withstand rigorous tests, including NIST randomness tests and a plethora of machine learning-based modeling attacks using both deep learning and classical machine learning methods. 

Five graduate students and three undergraduate students participated in the research, gaining experience and knowledge in a highly interdisciplinary research project that spans material synthesis, nanofabrication, hardware engineering, and computer security. The students have also gained various technical and professional skills that are essential to their future endeavors. 

In summary, this project demonstrates the feasibility of creating all-electric, silicon integrable, low-cost SPUFs with ideal properties as envisioned decades ago, which offers an alternative path for achieving strong security on highly resource-constrained devices.

abstractText:
This project develops a unique facility at Rice University that houses an ultracompact pulsed magnet combined with an arsenal of state-of-the-art instruments for materials research. A distinctive feature of this system is the combination of a strong magnetic field with ultrashort laser pulses covering a broad spectrum. This unconventional coupling of magnetism and optics can produce new scientific knowledge and exciting breakthroughs, advancing the frontier of materials physics and chemistry. With current collaborations with Japanese and French researchers, the novel facility positions Rice University as an international hub for materials researchers. The project also features a multifaceted workforce development plan run through the facility wherein graduate students receive hands-on experience in developing, fabricating, and disseminating miniature magnet models during classroom demonstrations. Workforce impact extends beyond the current project reaching an anticipated ~50 Ph.D. students over 10 years, thereby producing a new generation of rigorously educated and trained material scientists and engineers who are equipped with the technical expertise to advance fundamental and applied research well into the future.

The objective of this project is the development of a 50-Tesla ultrabroadband magneto-optical spectroscopy system, a unique facility that houses an ultracompact pulsed magnet combined with an arsenal of state-of-the-art instruments for modern materials, which has the potential to impact numerous technologies, including computation, communications, and sensing, in ways never before possible. The system combines a mini-coil magnet, an ultrafast ultrabroadband laser, and photodetection systems to develop various magneto-spectroscopic capabilities that will allow scientists to conduct transformative research. The system and research conducted therein provide new insights into the states, dynamics, and behaviors of electrons in unique materials that exhibit novel properties in high magnetic fields, including the spontaneous appearance of macroscopic coherence of excitons; nonequilibrium dynamics of Dirac fermions in a quantizing magnetic field; spin dynamics of strongly-interacting, one-dimensional electrons; states in high temperature superconductors; and magnon-polaritons. Team members are world leaders in an array of research areas: magneto-optical and ultrafast optical studies of low-dimensional systems, terahertz spectroscopy of nanomaterials, and theoretical and experimental condensed matter physics. The system is operated and maintained for Rice University researchers and external collaborators from around the world, making Rice a hub for an international network of materials researchers.

abstractText:
Since its arrival to the market, Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP) has transformed the field of HIV prevention. A once a day pill composed of conventional antiretrovirals repurposed for preventative use, research has proven PrEP to be highly effective in reducing individual risk of HIV infection. While studies have demonstrated PrEP’s therapeutic efficacy, the social effects of this therapeutic revolution across different groups and populations remains understudied. The research supported by this award uses ethnographic methods to investigate how different populations and individuals use PrEP, asking how the use of this drug effects individual practices, as well as perceptions of risk. In addition to providing funding for the training of a graduate student in anthropology in the methods of empirical, scientific data collection and analysis, the project will enhance scientific understandings of the social effects of HIV prevention strategies and therapies. 

The research will take place over 16 months in a context where PrEP has been made widely available through the production and distribution of a state manufactured generic. The researcher will work across four different community settings: a HIV policy institute, a private clinic, a community organization, and a selection of commercial and event venues that are significant to the local economy. Data will be collected through participant observation; interviews with health policy makers, doctors, community organizers, PrEP users, and other stakeholders; and focus groups and life histories of PrEP users from different population groups. Findings from this research will produce multi-perspective data needed by policy makers, public health practitioners, and social scientists to understand the factors that condition both access to and the broader experiences of these novel forms of therapy.

projectOutComesReport:
This project resulted in 18 months of fieldwork that was conducted primarily in Bangkok, Thailand from June 2021 thru December 2022. The goal of this fieldwork was to ethnographically document the therapeutic revolution surrounding PrEP, an oral prophylactic used to lower risk of HIV infection, exploring not only how the arrival of this new medical technology was changing community-based healthcare practice and service delivery, but also how it was affecting understandings of health, behavior, and identity among PrEP users themselves. Funding for this project supported recurrent interviews with PrEP users, as well as the collection of life histories and interviews with clinicians and staff from across a half a dozen relevant clinics and community-based care organizations.

Charting the social life of this drug, research from this fieldwork documents the myriad ways in which the effects of PrEP exceed its therapeutic bounds, impacting not only various individuals and communities' understandings of their health and sexual behaviors, but also provoking new forms of self-identity, as well as new political understandings around the relationship between pleasure, care, intimacy, work, and community. Through an anthropological analysis of how this drug is being used across clinical and non-clinical settings in the fashioning of new subjectivities and the reconfiguring of therapeutic relations, the research contributes to theory in both medical anthropology and science and technology studies (STS) that argues for social approaches to pharmaceuticals that see effect not as predetermined, but as configured through relations. By documenting the social lives of this HIV prevention drug, the research argues for an approach to drugs that is not limited to the substance itself, but that also accounts for the economic, social, political, and symbolic dimensions at play within any given context.  Furthermore, through the study's empirical engagement with the work of public health practitioners, the research also contributes to broader understandings of contemporary movements to manage the spread of HIV.

abstractText:
Part I: Non-technical description: 
Predicting how polar ice sheets will respond to future global warming is difficult because all the processes that contribute to their melting are not well understood. This is important because the more ice on land that melts, the higher sea levels will rise. The most significant uncertainty in current estimates of sea-level rise in the coming decades is the potential contribution from the Antarctic Ice Sheet. One way to increase our knowledge about how large ice sheets respond to climate change in response to natural factors is to examine the geologic past. Natural global warming (and cooling) events in Earth’s history provide examples that we can use to better understand processes, interactions, and responses we can’t directly observe today. One such time period, approximately three million years ago (known as the Pliocene), was the last time atmospheric carbon dioxide levels were as high as they are today and, therefore, represents a time period to study to better understand the ice sheet response to a warming climate. Specifically, this project is interested in understanding how ocean currents near Antarctica, which transport heat and store carbon, behaved during these past climate events. The history of past ice sheet-ocean interactions are recorded in sediments that were deposited, layer upon layer, in the deep sea offshore Antarctica. In January-February 2018, a team of scientists and crew set sail to the Ross Sea, offshore west Antarctica, on the scientific ocean drilling vessel JOIDES Resolution to recover such sediment archives. This project focuses on a sediment core from that expedition, which captures the relatively warm Pliocene time interval, as well as the subsequent transition into cooler climates typical of the past two million years. The researchers will analyze the sediment with multiple complementary measurements, including: grain size, composition, chemistry of organic matter, physical structures, microfossil type and abundance, and more. These analyses will be done by the research team, including several students, at their respective laboratories and will then integrated into a unified record of ice sheet-ocean interactions. Ultimately, the results will be used to improve modeled projections of how the Antarctic Ice Sheet could respond to future climate change. 

Part II: Technical description: 
Geological records from the Antarctic Ice Sheet (AIS) margin demonstrate that the ice sheet oscillated in response to orbital variations in insolation (i.e., ~400, 100, 41, and 20 kyr), and it appears to be more sensitive to specific frequencies that regulate mean annual insolation (i.e., 41-kyr obliquity), particularly when the ice sheet extends into marine environments and is impacted by ocean circulation. However, the relationship between orbital forcing and the production of Antarctic Bottom Water (AABW) is unconstrained. Thus, a knowledge gap exists in understanding how changing insolation impacts ice marginal and Southern Ocean conditions that directly influence ventilation of the global ocean. The researchers hypothesize that insolation-driven changes directly affected the production and export of AABW to the Southern Ocean from the Pliocene through the Pleistocene. For example, obliquity amplification during the warmer Pliocene may have led to enhanced production and export of dense waters from the shelf due to reduced AIS extent, which, in turn, led to greater AABW outflow. To determine the relationship of AABW production to orbital regime, they plan to reconstruct both from a single, continuous record from the levee of Hillary Canyon, a major conduit of AABW outflow, on the Ross Sea continental rise. To test their hypothesis, they will analyze sediment from IODP Site U1524 (recovered in 2018 during International Ocean Discovery Program Expedition 374) and focus on three data sets. (1) They will use the occurrence, frequency, and character of mm-scale turbidite beds as a proxy of dense-shelf-water cascading outflow and AABW production. They will estimate the down-slope flux via numerical modeling of turbidity current properties using morphology, grain size, and bed thickness as input parameters. (2) They will use grain-size data, physical properties, XRF core scanning, CT imaging, and hyperspectral imaging to guide lithofacies analysis to infer processes occurring during glacial, deglacial, and interglacial periods. Statistical techniques and optimization methods will be applied to test for astronomical forcing of sedimentary packages in order to provide a cyclostratigraphic framework and interpret the orbital-forcing regime. (3) They will use bulk sedimentary carbon and nitrogen abundance and isotope data to determine how relative contributions of terrigenous and marine organic matter change in response to orbital forcing. All of these data will be integrated with sedimentological records to deconvolve organic matter production from its deposition or remobilization due to AABW outflow as a function of the oscillating extent of the AIS. These data sets will be integrated into a unified chronostratigraphy to determine the relationship between AABW outflow and orbital-forcing scenarios under the varying climate regimes of the Plio-Pleistocene.

abstractText:
The rapid identification of pathogens is essential for clinical diagnostics and biodefense. Given timely information, clinicians can prescribe better treatments and slow the rise of drug resistant bacteria, and U.S. biosurveillance efforts can track the emergence and spread of both existing and newly evolved pathogens. While most rapid diagnostic tests have sensors that are each specialized to detect only one kind of pathogen, this research effort is developing new DNA sensing techniques to efficiently detect large numbers of pathogens with just a few sensors. By minimizing the number of necessary sensors, new pathogen surveillance devices could be portable and inexpensive for routine use.  The technology additionally provides an approach to detecting emerging novel pathogens without the need to create and deploy new test kits. In addition to furthering development of new pathogen identification technologies, the project develops a hands-on experimental module exploring this methodology and implements it in a biosensing and imaging course serving undergraduate and graduate engineering students at Rice University.  

This research effort applies compressed sensing which allows just a few DNA probes to (1) give each species a fingerprint response and (2) unmix these fingerprint signals when a few pathogens are in the same sample. Compressed sensing assumes that the sample is sparse. Sparsity occurs because although there may be dozens or hundreds of possible species to account for, any single sample from a patient or the environment will have only a few pathogens of interest for relevant applications. For pathogen detection, DNA probes each bind multiple times to microbial species. The number of binding events between a few probes and the microbes gives each of hundreds of species a “fingerprint” response, much like how 10 digits can give everyone in the U.S. a unique phone number. The first aim of this project is to develop a new DNA signal amplification technique that allows fewer binding events to be detectable. This amplification strategy also lets signals be positive or negative, effectively allowing fingerprint signals to spread further apart. The enhanced incoherence of the sensors is known to be very helpful for compressed sensing. The second aim is to use new technologies in microfluidics to capture individual pathogen cells in very small droplets and acquire fingerprint signals from each droplet separately. By analyzing every droplet, this project pushes towards single-cell resolution which would enable its broader application in any task that demands the characterization of unknown microbes.

projectOutComesReport:
The rapid, scalable identification of pathogens is essential for clinical diagnostics and biodefense. Modern devices are increasingly pressured to span hundreds of pathogens, and the time window for identification to inform treatment can be as low as six hours in cases of sepsis. Since sample culture can take several hours to days, clinicians are forced to preemptively initiate broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy even before confirming a bacterial agent. Clinicians would be empowered to select more targeted therapies and hamper the rise of drug resistance if timely pathogen identification was available. Through this award, we developed a thoroughly characterized framework for the combination of compressed sensing and microfluidic partitioning for scalable microbial diagnostics.  We developed an understanding of the framework’s scaling rules in theory and practice, as well as a sense of its practical limitations.   The framework facilitates accurate recovery for arbitrarily few sensors per droplet by leveraging both sparsity and the Poisson distribution of analyte capture in microfluidics. This result is particularly striking in the context of compressed sensing where it has always been theoretically necessary to use more sensors than the anticipated sparsity level of the sample.  Moreover, while our fundamental technology relies on “fingerprinting” microbes, we found that these fingerprints do not need to be fully resolved in every droplet. Capturing portions of the fingerprints in multiple groups of droplets helps break limitations often imposed by the number of resolvable sensors per droplet (e.g., limited fluorescence channels).  In summary, the techniques developed through this award empower sensor-constrained microfluidic systems to achieve scalable multiplexing, unlocking fundamentally new approaches to biosensing with commercially available and custom microfluidics systems.

abstractText:
Natural disasters, like hurricanes, tropical storms, and flood events, can generate massive amounts of debris, posing significant challenges to coastal communities. Financial and logistical burdens related to debris removal account for nearly a third of reimbursed recovery costs, and threats to public safety range from impaired emergency response to health hazards. There is need for more accurate models to estimate debris presence and quantities after, and preferably prior to a storm, so communities can better prepare for and manage debris burdens. Knowledge about what drives debris patterns is limited, so current predictive models are not accurate enough to support planning or response, particularly for multi-hazard storm events. In addition, coastal landscapes are constantly changing, and as development patterns shift so do prospective debris volumes and locations. This project addresses the need for integrative models that reflect the complex coupling between human-built-natural systems that underpin debris generation in storm events and the cascading impacts on coastal communities. This project examines the drivers of debris patterns and also develops models that couple those insights with infrastructure, socio-demographic, and human health impacts, among others. Resulting insights can inform policy decisions, coastal planning and risk mitigation, and debris management.  Synthesis of model outcomes and policy implications will be shared via web hosted interactive story mapping.

This project will transform our understanding of debris generation from coastal storms and its cascading consequences on communities by deriving coupled models of the interactions between human-built-natural systems. New methods will be developed for probabilistic modeling of debris presence and volumes, harnessing and fusing empirical data from past events, storm simulations, and physics-based estimates of fragility. A significant departure from traditional debris prediction models will be afforded by introducing nested statistical surrogate models informed by multi-resolution land use/land cover characteristics, physical vulnerability of structures or vegetation, and multi-hazard storm intensities. As a result, coupled models of development and debris potential are enabled for the first time to explore current and future storm risks and policy scenarios. By integrating models of the cascading consequences of debris with socio-demographic characteristics, this project will also shed new light on relationships between regional debris effects and social vulnerability that can inform future planning, management and mitigation efforts. Knowledge co-production and the practical viability of research methods will be advanced by working with stakeholders in testbed communities, to increase the likelihood that resulting models will be useful for future plans and decisions.

projectOutComesReport:
This project is focused on understanding and managing hurricane debris impacts in coastal areas, especially as storms intensify with climate change and sea level rise. The team developed reliable, data-driven models to predict debris from future hurricanes, analyze how development and urban planning affected debris distribution, and study how debris impacts transportation and access to emergency services, particularly in vulnerable communities. Key goals include integrating predictions about future conditions—like land cover changes, population growth, and storm severity—into the models to improve planning and resilience. with coastal communities and the engineering community to enhance understanding and encourage proactive disaster preparedness.

Major Achievements

Researchers have created sophisticated models that blend data-driven insights with physics-based approaches to simulate debris patterns during hurricanes, incorporating Hurricanes such as Ike (2008) and others as reference scenarios. These models account for future sea level rise, allowing the team to predict how debris patterns could change over time. By using deep learning and a high-resolution debris distribution model, they can accurately estimate debris volumes and locations on a regional scale, including projections of debris dynamics under different future scenarios. This provides critical insights into the cascading effects of debris, particularly on transportation infrastructure, which directly impacts community accessibility and response times during emergencies.

To further refine their predictions, the team evaluated future projections of socio-demographic variables, such as population trends and development patterns. This allows for better accuracy in estimating debris volumes and identifying critical areas for pre-event mitigation efforts and post-event debris management. These analyses enable the team to identify key areas where debris accumulation is most likely, allowing communities to prioritize their risk-informed decisions and resources more effectively.

Practical Implications for Resilience and Planning

By exploring the links between hurricane debris and the built environment, the project underscores the importance of urban planning in minimizing debris impacts. For instance, coastal areas with thoughtful urban design may experience reduced debris hazards, emphasizing how resilience can be influenced by development choices. The model’s insights guide decisions for coastal urban planning and infrastructure, helping communities anticipate and mitigate debris-related risks more effectively.

Educational and Professional Development

The project provided valuable training opportunities for graduate students in civil engineering and coastal management. Over the past year, the team has grown, bringing on students who have developed future hurricane scenarios and used geospatial analysis to study how climate change and land cover shifts influence debris impacts. One former Ph.D. student, who played a significant role in this project, transitioned to an academic career, crediting this experience with providing the skills and mentorship needed for success. A second Ph.D. student was supported by this project and just successfully defended his dissertation that included methodological skills gained during this effort. Undergraduate students also gained hands-on experience in applying deep learning and disaster resilience techniques to real-world problems, contributing to their technical growth and professional readiness.

Community Engagement and Data Sharing

To ensure that the research benefits both local and broader communities, the team actively shares their findings with a network of stakeholders. They have presented results through national and international conferences, reaching diverse audiences. Collaborative partnerships with key organizations, such as the Houston-Galveston Area Council and Harris County, have been central to this process, aligning the project’s goals with community needs in transportation planning, disaster management, and mitigation strategies. The project also contributes to federal initiatives through involvement with the Interagency Flood Risk Management group. By integrating regional data, such as future transportation and development plans, the team has been able to assess debris impacts under various future conditions, offering a realistic view of potential challenges for stakeholders.  All datasets and resources developed in the project are hosted on the NHERI Cyberinfrastructure DesignSafe-CI platform and will be shared publicly, promoting open access for future research and resilience planning.

This project exemplifies a multi-disciplinary approach to disaster research, combining engineering, data science, urban planning, and community engagement. By developing models that provide accurate, data-driven predictions, the project contributes to stronger, more informed coastal resilience strategies, helping communities face the growing challenges of a changing climate.

abstractText:
General audience abstract: 

Physicists have found that quantum mechanics works perfectly to describe the micro-world of single or small numbers of electrons, protons, or atoms.  Quantum correlations in these small systems, known as “quantum entanglement,” are the primary attribute driving the quest to realize quantum computation.  For a quantum computer to exhibit an advantage over an ordinary classical computer, however, the number of entangled particles must be large, thus presenting obstacles, both technical and fundamental, to their implementation.  NSF-funded graduate student researchers will perform experiments that explore the limits of quantum entanglement in the largest systems to date using self-stabilizing wavepackets of atoms, known as solitons.  Although large for a quantum system, containing as many as 10,000 atoms, solitons confined to a one-dimensional line are bestowed with a special robustness that makes them ideal for exploring how far quantum physics may be extended into the macro-world.  These experiments will help us understand the quantum/classical boundary, and how it may be extended to even larger systems.  By performing these experiments, graduate students, several from underrepresented groups, learn the methods of experimental atomic physics in a state-of-the-art laboratory, gaining expertise that will follow them in their careers in academia, government, or industry.
	
Technical audience abstract:

Solitons are dispersion-less excitations that arise in nonlinear systems.  They are found both in classical and quantum wave phenomena, such as waves propagating in water, plasmas, optical fibers, and in matter waves to name just a few examples.  Solitons are one of the few non-trivial systems that are described by an exactly integrable model. The researchers will continue their experimental investigation of bright matter-wave solitons produced from Bose-Einstein condensates with attractive interactions, and specifically, they will explore the role of integrability in determining the quantum/classical boundary.  Recent theory predicts that integrability will protect a macro/mesoscopic object from decoherence, and can lead to the observation of effects that are manifestly quantum in objects expected to be best described by mean-field theories.  By harnessing integrability, the effects of quantum fluctuations and quantum entanglement may be extended to systems with a large number of degrees of freedom, and which are large in physical size.  The research team has two specific goals:  1) to observe the integrability-breaking effect of quantum fluctuations on the binding of a higher-order soliton breather and 2) to study the fast and slow collision regimes of a fundamental soliton interacting with a repulsive barrier made from a light sheet, and to exploit this geometry to realize a matter-wave soliton interferometer.

projectOutComesReport:
One of the most striking aspects of quantum mechanics is entanglement.  Quantum entanglement is what caused Einstein to declare: “God doesn’t play dice!”  What got Einstein so excited is that entanglement leads to another famous flash point: “Spooky action at a distance”, and the topic, to this day, generates controversy.

Entanglement refers to a particular set of correlations that only applies to objects, or combinations of them, that are sufficiently small, to be … well, quantum!  We don’t know where the boundary is between the “classical” world and the quantum world.  We do know that two cows are big enough to be described according to Newton’s Laws of Physics, and so are two calves, two hairs, two protein molecules from the hair … In fact, experiments show that you need to take electrons off the back of the hot cow, and then, under the right conditions, you can observe quantum effects. 

This ability to interfere two objects of matter is related to the property called “coherence” and is what we aim to see in two Bose-Einstein condensates (although Einstein’s God doesn’t play dice, the two condensates do interfere with each other).  Coherence refers to how well two waves interfere.  It’s similar to  musical notes.  Imagine that you have two nearly identical tuning forks, such that each rings at a pure musical note when struck.  Hang the forks a couple of inches from each other and strike one of them...  after a while you should notice that the vibrations from the first one are transferred to the second one, at a frequency that depends on the difference of the two notes. 

The ability to see interference depends on the coherence between the two forks.  We have devised a way to learn where the boundary is between two Bose-Einstein condensates.  We expect that in our system the quantum/classical boundary may correspond to Bose-Einstein condensates composed of about 10,000 atoms. Measurements of coherence between two coupled Bose-Einstein condensates gives us the tool needed to probe the boundary.

abstractText:
Economists model the formation of relationships as the outcome of market forces using matching models. Matching models explain relationships such as marriage, employment, and business alliances. Most matching models are applied to relationships at a single point in time. However, relationships change over time and datasets tracking those changes are increasingly available. This project develops new methods, called repeated matching game, for studying how relationships change over time within a market framework.  The central idea is that in forming partnerships, people consider how current relationships affect their future relationships.  In addition to theory, the research project also develop new tools to analyze data for matching models.  The research applies the method to study marriage, divorce and remarriage, careers of engineers to learn how job assignment and moving among firms affect promotion to more prestigious roles.  The researchers also apply this model to study how early rounds of venture capital funding, including accelerator participation, raise the chance of receiving later rounds of funding and eventual startup success. The results provide inputs into matching decisions hence improve economic performance.

This project introduces the concept of a repeated matching game, where each period agents can make new matches. The forward-looking agents consider how their matches today will affect their abilities to make productive matches in the future. The repeated matching game combines a dynamic discrete choice model at the level of an individual agent with a per-time period, transferable utility matching game of relationship formation. The repeated matching game has desirable properties that lead to tractable equilibrium computation. The project extends knowledge about these matching models, develops computer algorithms for model solutions, and create new estimators for the model's parameters. The project develops empirical applications to marriage and remarriage, workers switching firms and venture capitalists funding startups.  The results of this research makes significant contribution to the matching game models as well provide some insights into labor market and other relationship policies.  The results provide inputs into matching decisions hence improve economic performance.

projectOutComesReport:
This project introduced a tractable model of one-to-one, two-sided dynamic matching. Relationship formation is pervasive in economics, and appears in a wide range of settings, such as marriage, labor or health care. Matching models are a key class of analytical tools that predict the formation of relationships. Consequently, they have become important empirical tools alongside the availability of datasets on formed relationships. In these models, agents on both sides on the market are paired based on their observable characteristics, or types. The value generated from a match, usually referred to as the match surplus, depends critically on the interaction of these types. For labor markets, where workers match with firms, the match surplus depends on the worker’s level of human capital and the firm’s productivity.

Many matching markets are dynamic in that they involve repeated interactions over time. Couples divorce and remarry, workers change jobs, and patients switch doctors – highlighting the dynamic nature of matching processes in real-world settings. However, much of the traditional literature, such as the celebrated Becker (1971) model of marriage, models matching at a point in time, treating each period as an independent market and abstracting away from potential intertemporal linkages. This overlooks an important feature of dynamic environments: while agents’ current types drive present matches, those matches, in turn, influence the future evolution of types. For example, a worker’s human capital evolves as a function of his or her employment history, implying that past matches shape future opportunities. Workers know this and account for this future change in their match decision.

In terms of intellectual merit, this project developed a model that explicitly incorporates this dynamic feedback into matching games with transferable utility, extending the classic static model of Shapley and Shubik (1971). Forward-looking agents have individual states that evolve with current matches. Agents are forward-looking and have complete information about their potential partners. They internalize how their current matching decisions affect the future trajectories of their types. The model results in a novel framework, repeated matching games. The solution concept in this model is a dynamic competitive equilibrium, which can be viewed as an extension of a Walrasian equilibrium to a dynamic setting with complete information.

In terms of theoretical results, the project proved the existence of an equilibrium with time-varying distributions of agent types and showed it is the solution to a social planner’s problem. The project also proved that a stationary equilibrium exists. The model was extended to introduce econometric shocks to account for unobserved heterogeneity in match formation. Analogous theorems to those just mentioned were proved for the model with econometric shocks.

The project introduced and benchmarked computational methods to compute both an equilibrium for the model with time-varying aggregate states as well as to directly compute a stationary equilibrium. For both the models with and without econometric shocks, the project computed the equilibrium matching for the time-varying aggregate state by solving the social planner’s Bellman equation for the planner’s value function. Also, the project introduced two new algorithms for computing a stationary equilibrium. One method, MPEC, solves a system of nonlinear equations using a nonlinear programming solver. The second method uses a primal-dual algorithm by Chambolle and Pock (2011). Benchmarks showed that both these methods can scale to problems with many agent types and the primal-dual algorithm scales better.

The project adapted both algorithms for estimation. Using one of these estimators, the project finally estimated a model of accumulation of job-specific human capital using panel data on Swedish engineers who work at private-sector employers. The project estimated match production as a function of worker and firm types, namely worker experience variables and the type of the job, technical or managerial. A worker’s occupation-specific experience in the past five years matters roughly four times more for matching into a general or managerial job over a technical job compared to overall potential experience in the labor market.

The above results have been distributed in a working paper that has been submitted to a leading journal in economics. The project’s results have been discussed at numerous conferences and university seminars and have formed the basis for new empirical work by a scholar not associated with the working paper. 

In terms of broader impacts, the project has made it easier to evaluate existing and proposed government policies in markets where relationships are important and agents change relationships over time. As an example, a researcher could evaluate the impacts of policies that change housing costs on labor market mobility between employers in different geographic locations. The project’s output could also be used to study policies that affect interfirm relationships, such as how tariffs affect interfirm international trade.

abstractText:
Anatoly Kolomeisky of William Marsh University is supported by an award from the Chemical Theory, Models and Computational Methods program in the Division of Chemistry to theoretically investigate the role of various chemical and biological processes. It is known that chemical reactions are random or stochastic processes, i.e., the times before the products appear are varied and broadly distributed. All living systems rely on a large number chemical reactions to support and maintain their activities.  The high efficiency of biological systems, however, raises a question of how random chemical reactions can lead to very precisely controlled biological processes. Professor Kolomeisky proposes that biological systems are able to properly tune the random chemical processes by utilizing several different mechanisms. By combining theoretical modeling, advanced computer simulations and extensive bioinformatics analysis, his research group investigates the mechanisms of various complex chemical and biological systems in order to clarify the role of randomness at the molecular level. Specific projects include: determination of the molecular origin of cell-size control in bacteria; understanding the mechanisms of transcription bursting; uncovering the role of motion in cancer initiation; and investigating the dynamics of heterogeneous catalytic chemical reactions. Close collaborations with experimental and theoretical groups enable testing of the new ideas on the role of randomness, and it promotes a deeper understanding of these complex natural processes.  Professor Kolomeisky is providing opportunities for high school and undergraduate students from underrepresented groups to participate in this research and gain valuable training and experience for their future careers. A special summer research program for visiting female and minority undergraduate students is established. Outreach activities also include the presentation of chemical shows in local schools, co-organization of an undergraduate chemistry research symposium, public lectures delivered at local cafes, and continued collaboration with science writers in order to disseminate the this knowledge to a general public.

Professor Kolomeisky focuses on developing a comprehensive theoretical description of stochastic effects in living cells by generating quantitative models for several specific biological and chemical phenomena. Theoretical analysis in his group is driven by a central hypothesis that cells are capable of tuning the randomness of biochemical reactions by using two main strategies, which involve a collective effect when many different stochastic processes are coupled together to cancel out the unfavorable random factors.  They also observe a coupling of stochastic processes with external fields (mechanical, electrical, etc.) to control the random features. Professor Kolomeisky will specifically investigate several biological and chemical processes in order to quantify the effect of stochasticity in each of them. These processes are analyzed using a variety of theoretical tools including discrete-state stochastic models, first-passage analysis, bioinformatics methods, and extensive Monte Carlo computer simulations. An outreach program developed by Professor Kolomeisky provides the opportunity for local high-school students and undergraduate students from underrepresented minority groups to participate in scientific research in an academic setting via special summer research programs. Professor Kolomeisky organizes a team of chemistry graduate students to give chemical experiments shows in local schools, which are supplemented by popular lectures in order increase the interests in STEM topics. The project also highlights the benefits of science for society by directly presenting scientific findings to the local community in an informal setting of café discussions, as well as communicating with science writers in local newspapers and participating in scientific internet blog discussions. The broader impacts of this project include a multidisciplinary training program for young researchers of different levels that will prepare them better for future technological and industrial challenges.

projectOutComesReport:
This was a theoretical proposal aimed to understand the role of stochasticity in microscopic mechanisms of chemical and biological processes. By utilizing a multi-scale approach that combined analytical calculations, numerical analysis, computer simulations, and machine-learning methods, we investigated  a variety of complex biological and chemical systems. Specifically, the following major findings are resulted from the studies supported by this proposal:

1)  A new theoretical framework to understand the molecular origin of cell-size regulation processes in bacteria has been developed. This fully quantiative approached not also explained all available experimental observations, but also allowed us to propose a concept of coupling of stochastic processes that might lead to previously unexplained very precise dynamics in cell-size regulation.

2) We developed a novel theoretical method to analyze transcription burting phenomena using mutli-state stochastic models. This provided the quantitative analysis of microscopic origin of transcription bursting and its role in the regulation of genetic transfer phenomena in living cells.

3) We presented a new theoretical approach to understand the dynamics of cancer initiation by concentrating on stochasticity of underlying phenomena. We were able to able multiple previously unexplained observations. Our main idea here is then analogy between cancer development and chemical reactions that opens new possibilities for developing new anti-cancer methods.

4)  A new theoretical approach for investigating catalysis phenomena have been proposed. The main idea here is that we concentrated in studying the dynamics of catalyzed chemical reactions since the dynamics reflects the underlying microscopic mechanisms. this allowed us to signficantly advance our understanding of the molecular mechanisms of catalysis, especially for the systems where nanopartilces play the role of catalysts.

5) We also developed a novel theoretical approach to understand the microscopic origin of secondary active transport in biological cells. The role of stochasticity is crucial here because these phenomena are supported by coupling thermodynamically unfavorable processes with thermodynamically favorable processes. Our chemicl-kinetic models clarified many aspects of these complex biological phenomena.

6) We also invetigated the molecular mechanisms of antimicrobial peptides and their combinations. By combining analytical models, computer simulations and machine-learning methods, we were able t clarify important aspects of their mechanisms.

Our multi-disciplinary studies involved 5 postdoctoral research associates and 4 graduate students. We also hosted several visitors from outside of USA, both students and senior researchers. The results of our studies have been published in more than 35 papers. 

Our theoretical studies advancd the knowledge of microscopic processes that are taking place in chemical and biological systems. They provided a multi-disciplinary training to students and other researchers, which prepared them better for future carrers in STEM fields. Some of the obtained results have been also included in teaching of Chemistry classes at Rice University. The results have been also disseminated to a broader non-scientific community via public lectures, presentations, school visits and online publications. This allowed us to emphasize the importance of fundamental science for the society.

title: Understanding the Role of Stochasticity in Chemical and Biological Processes

abstractText:
In the era of big data, complex data naturally arise in modern scientific applications. For example, the advance in computation and technology has enabled the routine collection of high-frequency functional data and high-resolution images. Scientists are facing daunting challenges from the data, including the massive scale, intricate dependence structures, and various shape constraints that are vital for scientific interpretability. This project will develop new flexible methods for shape-constrained regression and high-dimensional quantile regression to comprehensively depict the dependence between variables, with a focus on providing scalable implementation and theoretically guaranteed inference. These tools will address pressing statistical and computational challenges, leading to broad applications in medicine, neuroscience, cancer-related studies, and industrial settings. The project will also develop and distribute open-source software and provide research opportunities for undergraduate and graduate students. 

The project will develop novel semiparametric methods for high-dimensional quantile regression and shape-constrained regression. The PI will investigate a paradigm shift in high-dimensional regression from a joint, iterative scheme to a two-step, distributed scheme. This strategy allows the utilization of parallel computation and is coupled with proper uncertainty propagation to ensure statistical optimality and frequentist coverage of simultaneous confidence and credible bands. Several regimes using functional and image data will be considered, for example, mean regression, quantile regression, and variable selection. The project will also develop new methods for nonparametric regression under shape constraints, including local sparsity and stationary points of unknown functions. The project will enrich the statistical toolbox to cope with complex data by developing a suite of semiparametric methods that are theoretically sound and computationally efficient.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

projectOutComesReport:
In the realm of big data analytics, scalability and interpretability continue to be pressing challenges across a wide range of scientific fields. This project addresses these challenges by focusing on two fronts: developing scalable quantile regression methods to capture heterogeneity in high-frequency functional data, and advancing shape-constrained regression techniques to enhance scientific interpretability.

In this project, we have proposed new methods with theoretical guarantees. In particular, we have developed semiparametric methods tailored for high-dimensional quantile regression. Through a two-step, distributed scheme, we have enabled the use of parallel computation, which not only accelerates the computation but also ensures optimal estimation accuracy and facilitates statistical inference. In the pursuit of interpretability, we have developed methods for nonparametric regression and functional data analysis subject to interpretable shape constraints. These techniques improve our ability to detect local sparsity and stationary points of unknown nonparametric functions in intricate datasets.

The advancements brought about by this project have substantially enriched the statistical tools available to researchers, offering solutions that are both theoretically sound and computationally efficient. This project addresses critical needs in fields where understanding intricate data dependence with interpretability is essential--for instance, in medical research using mass spectrometry proteomics for pancreatic cancer studies, and in neuroscience using electroencephalography data for understanding human language processing.

The project has made contributions to the scientific community by releasing open-source software, thus widening the accessibility of these methods. It has also supported educational development by providing research opportunities for students at the undergraduate and doctoral levels, as well as by supplying teaching materials.

abstractText:
Gigabit-per-second scale wireless transmission is already commercially available in wireless local area networks (WLANs). For example, the latest Wi-Fi standard at 60 gigahertz promises data rates up to 100 gigabits per second The  objective of this project is to realize the next order of magnitude in data rate, spectrum access, directionality, and spatial multiplexing targeting terabit per second WLANs with a low-latency control plane that supports mobile clients.  Namely, scaling spectrum access towards terahertz will provide a key ingredient to realize the sixth generation of wireless networks. Thus, this project will result in the design, implementation, and proof-of-concept demonstration of a WLAN architecture using spectrum from 100 gigahertz to 500 gigahertz with range exceeding 100 meters.

This project targets to scale multi-stream data rates to terabit per second for mobile clients via the following integrated research thrusts. The first project thrust provides two underlying building blocks for steerable and highly directional beams from 100 GHz to 500 GHz: (1) A first-of-its-kind pixelated metasurface waveguide will be developed to dynamically steer a THz beam via electrical switching of the meta-elements.  (2) A THz leaky waveguide's unique property of coupling frequency and steering angle will be exploited for the first time to provide frequency-selective adaptive beam steering.  The second project thrust targets scaling to high-density user populations.  First, new smart reflecting surfaces will  be developed that will enable engineered non-specular non-line-of-sight paths. This thrust will experimentally study the achievable network density under different architectural components, identifying empirical limits at THz scale of packing many simultaneous physical links into a limited spatial area. The third project thrust targets to provide uninterrupted Tb/sec scale communication even in the presence of user and environmental mobility.  The project's methodology aims to scale the control plane to a large and dense mobile WLAN via a novel spectral signature for each transmission and reception angle. Namely, with a terahertz rainbow emitted from a leaky waveguide, a unique angular signature is derived for each path, whether line of sight, a specular reflection, or an engineered path.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

Intellectual Merit 

Gigabit-per-second scale wireless transmission is already commercially available in wireless local area networks (WLANs). For example, the latest Wi-Fi standard at 60 gigahertz promises data rates up to 100 gigabits per second. This project has made critical contributions towards realizing the next order of magnitude in data rate, spectrum access, directionality, and spatial multiplexing targeting terabit per second WLANs. Importantly, our efforts involved the conception, design, and evaluation of wireless communication, sensing, and security methods, as well as the supporting hardware architecture, to leverage the wireless spectrum of 100 gigahertz to 500 gigahertz. We have conducted our research under three major thrusts, with notable accomplishments from each described below.

Our first thrust focused on engineering how the electromagnetic waves propagate through space in the mentioned frequency range. In stark contrast to wireless communication signals below 60 gigahertz, these high-frequency waves exhibit considerably more power loss as they travel through air and other materials, requiring smart use of transmitting and receiving device characteristics to enable terabits per second data rates within a reasonable power budget. In pursuit of this goal, we designed several methods that shape the propagation of the high-frequency waves to maximize signal quality at the receiver while avoiding physical obstacles in the environment. Notable methods designed and experimentally demonstrated under this project thrust include capacity-maximizing beam focusing, curving wireless links around obstacles, self-healing beams, and high-level protocols that switch between such methods according to the ever-changing wireless communication environment.

Our second thrust involved our efforts towards scaling to high-density user populations by serving multiple wireless users through the same Access Point (AP) simultaneously, a powerful paradigm to minimize latency and maximize the aggregate data rate of the network. As the conventional wireless communication hardware is yet to be successfully adapted to these high frequencies, we have designed and experimentally evaluated numerous architectures that not only enable the use of this high-frequency spectrum, but also unlock multi-user communication with strong emphasis on maintaining signal quality at each user. Notable architectures realized under this thrust include our metasurface-based multi-user symbol optimizing system and our tilted leaky-wave antenna arrays.

Finally, our third project thrust has made advancements towards enabling uninterrupted terabits per second communication even the wireless users and other entities in the environment are mobile. As described in our first thrust, the physical locations of these users and entities in the environment are critical to the reliability of a wireless link at these high frequencies, as the extreme power loss of the propagating signal requires it to be transmitted in a location-aware manner. In this thrust, we developed techniques to ensure such location-awareness can be maintained through the entire duration of the established wireless link, even when the users (or the obstacles) move, so that the degradation in signal quality can be minimized. Notable methods designed and demonstrated in line with this goal include (i) a terahertz leaky waveguide that creates an electromagnetic dispersion pattern similar to the phenomenon observed when white light passes through an optical prism (ii) a transmissive surface creating random wave patterns that act as “spatial fingerprints” for each wireless user in the environment.

Broader Impacts 

With a forward-looking approach, our research under this project focused on designing and experimentally demonstrating novel terahertz devices and structures. By exploring the potential of THz technology, we envision a wide range of applications in various fields in addition to wireless communications, including healthcare, automation, and agriculture.

In addition to the echoing impact of our work on technological advancements, the principal investigators of our research have made substantial educational contributions by delivering numerous seminar sessions and tutorials on terahertz communications, sensing, and

security at esteemed conferences and workshops. Their expertise and insights have been shared with the wider research community, furthering knowledge in these critical areas. As part of our effort to raise awareness and enhance the national impact of our research, the principal investigators participated in organizing a workshop through the Engineering Research Visioning Alliance (ERVA), an NSF-sponsored consortium. Subsequent to the workshop, the team produced a report entitled “Strategic Engineering for Next-Generation Wireless Competitiveness,” which was publicly released in the spring of 2025, available at http://ervacommunity.org.

Our commitment to open research and knowledge sharing is reflected in our published manuscripts and publicly available resources. As such, we foster a culture of sharing and collaboration, collectively pushing the boundaries of knowledge and driving further innovation in the field we are passionate about.

abstractText:
With the decline in year-over-year performance increases achieved by new general-purpose processors, a growing variety of devices, e.g., field-programmable gate arrays, are being added to computers to accelerate applications.  Consequently, the operating system (OS) must not only manage access to the computer's memory by applications running on general-purpose processors but also on a diverse array of accelerators.  Currently, memory access by these accelerators is managed by different, disconnected parts of the OS, leading to a proliferation of independent, redundant, and often inefficient implementations.  This project aims to replace the current fragmented architecture by a unified framework for all devices.

Specifically, this project's principal objective is to create a generalized mapping and protection system, called Gmem, that will provide a single, consistent interface within the OS for the creation, management, and destruction of mappings to any physical memory across all devices.  Gmem will simplify the overall architecture of the mapping system within the OS. It will enable the authors of device drivers to implement just the device-specific behavior that they need, rather than implementing a complete mapping system.  Furthermore, Gmem will provide asynchronous interfaces and employ coupled page table management, which together will enable high performance and strong protection.

In its never-ending quest for increased performance, the computing community should expect to see the continued rise of specialized accelerators, increased integration with graphics processing units, networking interfaces, and storage devices, and large amounts of non-volatile memory across the computing system.  This conglomeration of components in next generation computing systems requires OS designers to rethink the ways in which the OS manages disparate memory.  A broader impact of this project is that it will contribute to the significant innovations in OS software that will be needed to realize the full potential of these systems.

Software artifacts and experimental data of long-term value that are created for this project will be available at https://github.com/rice-systems/gmem for at least three years beyond the project's end.

projectOutComesReport:
There has been a proliferation of devices in modern computing systems that require address space management. The operating system (OS) no longer simply maintains the virtual-to-physical address mappings for the processes running on the system using a single page table structure for each process. Instead, the OS now must manage the address spaces for virtual machines, I/O devices, accelerators, GPUs, non-volatile memory, and other components of the system. These diverse components have been managed with independent, disconnected parts of the OS, leading to a proliferation of virtual address space management, physical memory management, and mapping systems.

Sometimes the virtual address space is unique for each device; other times a uniﬁed address space is shared across devices. The physical memory has been largely consolidated within the central processing unit (CPU) complex, but is increasingly distributed across devices. And the page table format and synchronization mechanisms are largely unique across devices. This makes somewhat simple-seeming OS tasks extremely complicated. For example, if the OS wants to destroy all of the mappings to a speciﬁc physical page in memory, it now potentially has to be aware of every subsystem that might hold a mapping to that page and destroy each mapping in a device-speciﬁc way.

Furthermore, as each new device is added to the system, the device and OS developers have been "reinventing the wheel" to build address space managers, memory allocators, and mapping managers. These systems are often suited to the unique characteristics of the device, but are still accomplishing the same fundamental tasks.

Finally, the current architecture can lead to security issues. For example, modern systems typically expose memory to I/O devices via the I/O memory management unit (IOMMU) long after that memory should be unmapped. This is largely due to the performance limitations of the current mapping management system's interface that requires unmap operations to be synchronous for correctness. Given the large performance penalty, most modern operating systems instead choose to expose memory which leads to real security vulnerabilities.

This project has proposed Generalized MEmory Management (GMEM) for devices. GMEM provides centralized memory management for computer systems with heterogeneous memory resources. Specifically, GMEM introduces three key innovations. First, GMEM provides a high-level interface within the OS for the management of memory across all devices. This enables devices to leverage the OS's memory management subsystem effectively.  Each device driver only needs to implement the device-specific code that is necessary to enable the OS to interact with the hardware, rather than inventing a completely new memory management system for every device. Second, GMEM leverages the functionality and optimizations within the virtual memory (VM) management system across devices. Therefore, as the OS integrates additional capabilities and performance optimizations, GMEM-based device drivers automatically benefit. Finally, GMEM enables the use of a single address space across the CPU and devices. This improves the programmability of accelerators, as GMEM's internal coordination mechanisms perform the necessary memory management tasks, freeing the programmer from worrying about address space coordination.

The effectiveness of GMEM was demonstrated using several case studies. For example, converting FreeBSD's IOMMU driver to use GMEM eliminates the need for a special-purpose I/O virtual address (IOVA) allocator. This eliminates over six hundred lines of code and reduces the chance of performance bugs. Furthermore, as GMEM integrates separate memory optimizations, the GMEM-based IOMMU driver receives automatic performance improvements. Experiments show that a GMEM-based driver obtains 54% higher network receive throughput while utilizing 32% less CPU than mainline Linux. Simultaneously, the GMEM-based IOMMU driver enables line rate transmit throughput at 40 Gbps with 45% less CPU utilization than Linux. As another example, an Intel graphics processing unit (GPU) driver was modified to use GMEM. GMEM integrates a memory optimization that speeds up zeroing larger pages, which reduces the GPU kernel launch time by 45%.

GMEM can also simplify driver development. The drivers of two simulated GPUs take less than 70 lines of code to implement their device memory management, excluding the memory management unit (MMU) functions. Applications can quickly be developed for these simulated devices within a single address space and they can execute seamlessly with smaller device memory capacity. These case studies demonstrate that GMEM enables device drivers to take better advantage of existing and future devices, provides more functionality, and improves performance. More importantly, the OS now has centralized control of heterogeneous memory resources enabled by GMEM's internal coordination. This lays the foundation for better global resource utilization in systems incorporating multiple types of accelerators.

abstractText:
Rice University researchers engaged in groundbreaking data-intensive science and engineering increasingly depend on access to real-time data analysis facilities required for their research. These research activities include image processing, computer vision, and machine learning, spanning multiple fields, such as geological sciences, statistics, computer science, and physics. Each of these problems areas or use cases can be addressed by shared computational infrastructure leveraging GPU accelerators for interactive computing. The system provides a significant resource for enabling science but also for educating the next generation of computational scientists in the latest GPU-computing techniques through the outreach of the Center for Research Computing. 

The resource includes nine compute nodes, each with 40 cores, 384GB RAM, 4TB NVMe storage, and 8 NVIDIA Quadro RTX 6000 GPUs. The systems are interconnected via high-performance networking and hosted on a Science DMZ integrating them with the Open Science Grid as well as commercial cloud allowing both increased utilization as part of national OSG efforts and the ability to utilize cloud resources for load bursting. The system leverages an open-source software stack designed to support containerization, enabling each researcher to utilize their own unique set of software and toolkits while sharing common hardware and a common cloud access platform. Moreover, the infrastructure is part of a larger technology ecosystem that leverages federated identity and access management as part of InCommon, advanced networking with science DMZ, and Information Security Office that supports not only university data and technology security but includes targeted outreach for research data and protocol security.

projectOutComesReport:
The Rice Analysis Platform for Interactive Data (RAPID) was designed to address the increasing demands for real-time data analysis by researchers at Rice University. In order to satisfy the goal of providing interactive computing resources, RAPID was implemented as a hybrid cloud with systems hosted on a Science DMZ network at Rice University as well as temporary resources available from a commercial cloud provider for satisfying periods of high demand. Utilizing software container orchestration addressed both the challenge of presenting a simplified user experience for such a distributed resource as well as providing the various specialized software environments required by the research community. The OpenNebula platform was chosen to centralize management of the local and remote systems.

This award funded core campus computing infrastructure consisting of 10 systems totaling 448 CPU cores, 5TB RAM, 16x NVIDIA A100 GPUs, and 64x NVIDIA A40 GPUs, connected via 100Gb networking. Local uses for the system have included signal and image processing research, development of resource aware machine learning algorithms, and molecular dynamics simulation analysis across multiple science domains. The interactive nature of the resource has made it especially well suited for software development as well as new user training. A baseline 20% of the local CPU and GPU cycles and any additional cycles available during periods of reduced local demand have been allocated to the Open Science Grid’s Open Science Pool, allowing the national science and engineering community access to the resource.

abstractText:
This Smart & Connected Communities (S&CC) planning grant will lay the foundation for a new paradigm of “Smart Resilience” in which data emerging from smart systems is leveraged to improve the hazard resilience of communities. As modern cities are becoming increasingly smart and interconnected, a wealth of emerging data (e.g. camera, sensors, crowdsourced reports) poses both challenges and opportunities for enhancing resilience to natural hazards, such as flooding, which threaten the safety, prosperity and wellbeing of communities. In this planning grant the focus is on the short-term response phase of the “Smart Resilience” paradigm (during and immediately following a hazard event) and emphasize organizational impacts. A new framework will be advanced, SSSAFT (Smart Systems for Situational Awareness of Flood Impacts and Transportation Access). This framework leverages data from smart systems to support situational awareness of community organizations responsible for flood resilience decision-making. Target organizations are those responsible for emergency response, flood risk communication surrounding transportation safety, and healthcare services. Through a convergent project design, this planning grant will lay a foundation for disciplinary integration, offer the opportunity for data collection and data fusion, launch testbeds, and provide the community context and opportunity for knowledge co-production with stakeholders. Integration with local partners, new knowledge shared with the research community, and submission of an award that builds off this planning grant are expected by the end of the project.     

This project harnesses expertise from Hydrology, Infrastructure Risk Modeling, Data Science and Machine Learning, and Organizational Psychology to derive methods for transforming situational awareness tools and understanding how this awareness can facilitate organizational functioning toward improved community resilience. Three key research questions are examined in this planning grant. First, data sources and technologies are explored that underpin future situational awareness tools to support smart resilience in flood prone communities. In question two the need for a probabilistic approach to generate intelligent information on flood condition and transportation access across communities is probed. Methods for information fusion are tested, forming the basis of a SSSAFT framework that can evaluate, for example, access to critical facilities or travel times to vulnerable populations. Finally, quantitative and qualitative information is collected via interviews and surveys to uncover the psychological and physical effects of incorporating SSSAFT into resilience-related decision processes and communications. This work will reveal how timely situational awareness affects organizational psychological resilience and the subsequent well-being of community members who depend on these first-response organizations.
